key_facts: **Melanocytic naevi (moles)** are benign clonal proliferations of melanocytes; most adults have 10–40.
They evolve over life: **junctional** (flat) → **compound** (raised) → **intradermal** (soft, skin-coloured), and many fade after middle age.
Common naevi are symmetrical, one or two colours, under about 6 mm, and match the person's other moles ('signature' naevi).
Dermoscopy patterns (reticular, globular, homogeneous) help; the **ugly duckling** and changing lesion need assessment.
Reassure typical naevi; refer any lesion meeting the NICE 7-point checklist or with clinical concern via the **suspected cancer pathway**.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Benign clonal proliferations of melanocytes ("moles"). They appear from early childhood and peak in number in the 20s–30s (a typical white adult has 10–40). Many involute after 50.

Dermoscopy (epiluminescence microscopy) shows structures in the epidermis and papillary dermis. In trained hands it raises sensitivity for melanoma by roughly 10–30% over the naked eye. In untrained hands it may not improve accuracy.
Common patient questions about whether contraception, pregnancy, HRT or sunbeds change moles or melanoma risk.

sub: Naevi appear in childhood, peak in number in the 20s–30s and decline after 50.
More naevi with fair skin, childhood sun exposure and family history; acral naevi more common in darker skin.
More than about 100 naevi, or several atypical naevi, is a major melanoma risk factor; most melanomas still arise de novo, not in a pre-existing mole.

ul: Most acquired naevi carry **BRAF V600E**, and congenital naevi carry **NRAS** mutations. After growth they enter **oncogene-induced senescence**, which is why most never become melanoma.

**Life cycle:** **junctional** (nests at the dermo-epidermal junction; flat, brown) → **compound** (junctional + dermal; raised centre) → **dermal (intradermal)** (dermal only; soft, skin-coloured to light-brown dome, often hair-bearing; adults).

Drivers of naevus number: genetics (MC1R, family), **childhood sunburn and intermittent UV**, immunosuppression, BRAF inhibitors (eruptive naevi), and pregnancy/hormones (darkening rather than true growth in most cases).
Somatic **BRAF V600E** (common naevi) or **NRAS** (congenital naevi) mutations start a clone, which then stops growing (oncogene-induced senescence).
Sun exposure in childhood and genetics (number of naevi is strongly inherited).
**"Moles turn into cancer"**: individual moles rarely do; the number of moles signals risk.
**"Hairs mean it's safe"**: hair does not exclude melanoma.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A naevus is a clone of melanocytes that grows, then **switches itself off**.

mech.t: A melanocyte acquires a **BRAF** or **NRAS** mutation and proliferates as nests at the dermo-epidermal junction (junctional naevus).
After a growth phase, the clone enters **oncogene-induced senescence** (p16) and stops enlarging: a stable mole.
Nests drop into the dermis (compound, then intradermal naevus); deeper cells become smaller and less pigmented.
mech.caption: Life cycle of a naevus: junctional → compound → intradermal, then fading.

mech.t: Many naevi fade or become fibrous in older age; a new or changing pigmented lesion in an adult needs more caution.

blocks: Pigment depth predicts colour: black is in the stratum corneum or epidermis; brown is at the dermo-epidermal junction; blue-grey is in the dermis (Tyndall effect). Network = pigmented rete ridges; globules = nests.

ul: **COCP:** large meta-analyses show **no meaningful increase in melanoma risk**. Melanocytes express oestrogen receptors, and darkening of naevi or melasma can occur.

**Pregnancy:** naevi may darken or enlarge on the abdomen and breasts (skin stretch). **Changing naevi in pregnancy still need assessment**, and pregnancy-associated melanoma is not more aggressive stage-for-stage, but diagnosis is often delayed.

**HRT:** observational studies show at most a small association. **No requirement to stop HRT** because of moles. The course "stop HRT if lesions increase" is not standard UK advice (see *Where course teaching differs from UK guidance*). Review the overall benefit-risk with the patient. For **people with a history of melanoma**, HRT is not contraindicated in most guidance (individualise with the oncology team).

**Sunbeds:** **IARC Group 1 carcinogen.** Ever-use raises melanoma risk by ~20%, and **first use before 35 raises it by ~60–75%** (Boniol 2012; Colantonio 2014). Use also accelerates photoageing, and the risk rises with the number of sessions. [Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi) (3×/week for 18 months, about 230 sessions) represents substantial exposure.

histo: Junctional: nests at the dermo-epidermal junction; compound: junctional plus dermal nests; intradermal: dermal nests only, showing **maturation** with depth.
No atypia, symmetry and orderly maturation separate naevi from melanoma.

sections.title: Clinical features

head: Type
Look
Photo
rows: Slightly raised, brown, may have a flat rim
Soft, dome-shaped, skin-coloured or pink-tan; may have a few fine vessels; face, trunk
Symmetrical, regular border, one or two colours

blocks: **Benign change:** a slow gradual elevation of a naevus with age (junctional → dermal), lightening, and evenly spread darkening in pregnancy or adolescence.

ul: **Reticular**: a regular network that fades at the periphery (junctional/compound; trunk).
**Globular**: regular brown globules (compound/dermal, children and young adults; the **[Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi)** pattern).
**Homogeneous** (blue = blue naevus; tan = dermal naevus).
**Starburst**: symmetrical peripheral streaks, typical of a pigmented Spitz/Reed naevus (in adults it needs excision because it mimics melanoma).
**Mixed reticular-globular** with symmetry.
Dermal naevus vessels: **comma vessels, out of focus** ("hazy", because they are deeper).

blocks: Atypical network, irregular streaks, irregular dots/globules (especially peripheral), blue-white veil, regression structures (white scar-like, peppering), negative network, atypical vessels (dotted, polymorphous), and more than one pattern asymmetrically.

**Naevus vs BCC** (the course [Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi) point): **BCC arborising vessels are bright red and sharply in focus** on the surface, and there is **no pigment network**. Dermal naevus vessels are comma-shaped and blurred, with residual globules or homogeneous tan.

ul: **Sunbeds (Regulation) Act 2010**: **under-18s are banned** from using sunbeds in commercial premises. Scotland (Public Health etc. (Scotland) Act 2008 and the 2009 regulations) and Northern Ireland (Sunbeds Act (NI) 2011) have equivalent bans, plus supervision and information requirements. At 19, [Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi) is legally entitled to use them, so counselling is the lever.
**Mole mapping:** total-body photography ± sequential digital dermoscopy (specialist or private). Most useful for high-risk people (AMS, FAMMM), and it reduces unnecessary excisions.

**Smartphone apps and AI:** many consumer apps are unregulated or have poor sensitivity. Under UK MDR 2002 and MHRA rules, apps that diagnose are medical devices. Some UKCA/CE-marked AI tools, e.g. **DERM (Skin Analytics)**, are used *within* NHS teledermatology pathways with dermatologist oversight. NICE early value assessment HTE24, now HealthTech guidance **HTG746**, supports **conditional use of DERM** for triaging adults already referred on the urgent suspected skin cancer pathway, with evidence generation over 3 years. People with black or brown skin (Fitzpatrick V–VI) need healthcare-professional review.

blocks: False reassurance is the main harm. Amelanotic and nodular melanomas are often missed by both apps and ABCDE.

sub: Naevi may darken slightly, but a clearly changing mole needs the same assessment as at any other time.
New naevi are normal; childhood melanoma is rare and often amelanotic or nodular (use modified ABCD criteria).

ul: History of change (who noticed it, over what time, photos?), the **NG12 weighted 7-point checklist**, the **ABCDE** rule, and the **"ugly duckling" sign**. See the [describing skin lesions](condition:lesion-language) notes.
**Dermoscopy** (trained clinician; see *Dermoscopy of naevi; naevus vs BCC; biopsy rules*).
**Excision biopsy** (2 mm margin, full thickness) if melanoma cannot be excluded.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Melanoma
ddx.f: Change, asymmetry, multiple colours; EFG nodule.

ddx.name: BCC
ddx.f: Pink pearly, for a pink dermal naevus.

blocks: Melanoma (SSM or nodular), SK, dermatofibroma, BCC (pigmented or nodular, for a pink dermal naevus), neurofibroma (soft, buttonhole sign), and molluscum.
See *Acquired melanocytic naevi* and the [melanoma](condition:melanoma) notes.
See *Acquired melanocytic naevi* and *Dermoscopy of naevi; naevus vs BCC; biopsy rules*. Melasma, pregnancy-related hyperpigmentation and new SKs are non-naevus differentials.

ul: **Apply the NG12 weighted 7-point checklist:** Major features (2 points each): change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour; Minor features (1 point each): diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation; **≥3 points → suspected cancer pathway** (NG12 1.7.1); **Below 3: still refer if there is any concern** (the score is a minimum, not a ceiling)

**[Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi):** change in size = 2, which is below 3. But the history is a growing mole in a heavy sunbed user. If the IP cannot confidently diagnose a dermal naevus with dermoscopy, **refer** (routine dermatology or teledermatology with dermoscopic) and **photograph with a ruler**.

**Cosmetic removal** of benign naevi is generally not NHS-funded. Shave removal of a dermal naevus for cosmetic reasons is private and done by a dermatologist or surgeon who sends the specimen for histology.
**Use dermoscopy only if trained and competent.** Otherwise send good dermoscopic images via teledermatology (many ICSs run "photo-triage" for 2WW skin referrals) or refer.

**Biopsy rules for suspected melanoma:** **excision biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin and a cuff of fat**, oriented along the limb's long axis (to preserve options for wide local excision and SLNB). **Do not shave, punch or incise** a suspected melanoma or a naevus of uncertain nature in primary care, because partial biopsy risks sampling error and makes Breslow thickness impossible to measure. Exceptions (specialist only): large facial lentigo maligna or acral/nail lesions, where incisional biopsy is accepted.
The NICE IOG says that **lesions suspected of melanoma should be referred, not excised, in primary care**.
**COCP:** continue. No need to change the method because of moles. Melasma on the COCP: consider a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method if it is troublesome (UKMEC).

**Sunbed counselling (NICE NG34 and NICE PH32 on skin cancer prevention):** explain the risk with concrete numbers. Use brief-intervention techniques (relate to appearance; photoageing and "self-tan alternatives"); **fake tan / DHA products are safe alternatives but do not protect** against UV. Sun protection: shade 11:00–15:00, clothing, SPF 30+ with 4–5-star UVA, reapply.
**Vitamin D:** heavy UV avoidance should not lead to deficiency. Consider 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily, especially October–March (NICE NG34/PH56).

Recommend **monthly self-examination** with dated, rather than relying on an unregulated app. **A reassuring app result never overrides clinical concern.** Conversely, an app "flag" alone justifies professional review, not panic (the [melanoma](condition:melanoma) notes [Case 1](condition:melanocytic-naevi)).

**Lifestyle:** sun protection, no sunbeds, stop smoking (general health; not a melanoma risk factor), vitamin D. **Diet and supplements do not prevent melanoma**, although nicotinamide does prevent keratinocyte cancer in high-risk patients (the [skin cancer](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) notes). Evidence for nicotinamide in melanoma prevention is lacking.

blocks.h: Case 1: 19-year-old woman, long-standing back mole growing over 6 months; sunbeds 3×/week for 18 months; COCP

ul: **Diagnosis (course teaching, from the lost):** benign **dermal (intradermal) naevus**. Dermoscopy: globular/homogeneous pattern with blurred (out-of-focus) comma vessels, **not** the sharp arborising vessels of BCC.
**Management:** reassurance + **sunbed and sun-protection counselling** + self-monitoring with; continue the COCP. **Never partially biopsy** a naevus.

**UK IP caveat:** NG12 score = 2 (change in size), below the threshold. But without competent dermoscopy, **refer** (teledermatology with dermoscopic, or routine dermatology) rather than reassure. The under-18 sunbed ban doesn't apply; counselling does.

blocks.h: Case 2: 5-year-old, 30 cm trunk CMN becoming darker, rougher, larger

ul: **Diagnosis:** large → **giant** (projected adult size >40 cm) congenital melanocytic naevus.
**Melanoma risk:** roughly 2–5% lifetime overall for large/giant (up to 10–15% with satellites/multiple CMN). The course 5–10% sits in this range. **Small/medium CMN: <1%.**

**Plan:** paediatric dermatology for **lifelong surveillance**; urgent review of any nodule; MRI if multiple CMN or neurological signs; MDT decisions about surgery (which does not reduce melanoma risk); psychological support. Roughness and hairiness are benign maturation.

blocks.h: Case 3: 30-year-old PE teacher, mother had melanoma, blistering childhood sunburn

ul: **Diagnosis:** atypical naevus syndrome. **FAMMM** if ≥2 affected relatives (or a CDKN2A mutation).
**Risk:** substantially raised. >100 naevi is significant; course teaching gave a lifetime risk of ~15%. CDKN2A carriers carry much higher risk.

**Plan:** dermatology for dermoscopy + total-body photography + **digital follow-up every 6–12 months**; consider genetics (ask about pancreatic cancer); self-examination; sun protection at work; no sunbeds.

ladder.t: Major (2): change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour. Minor (1): ≥ 7 mm, inflammation, oozing, sensation change. **≥ 3 → suspected cancer pathway**; **< 3: still refer if any concern** (a minimum, not a ceiling).
Can’t confidently call it benign with dermoscopy → refer (routine / teledermatology) with dermoscopic images and a ruler.
Cosmetic removal generally not NHS-funded; specimens always to histology.
No sunbeds (**illegal < 18**); SPF ~2 mg/cm² (6–8 teaspoons whole body), reapply; monthly self-checks with photos.

refer.t: 7-point score **≥ 3** or strong suspicion: suspected cancer pathway.
Ugly duckling or a **new mole after 40**: low threshold to refer.
New / eruptive naevi on immunosuppression or BRAF inhibitors that look atypical.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: NICE weighted 7-point checklist score of **3 or more**, or strong suspicion: **suspected cancer pathway** referral (NG12).
A mole that stands out from the patient’s others (ugly duckling), or a new mole after 40: low threshold to refer.
Under-18s cannot legally use sunbeds in the UK (Sunbeds (Regulation) Act 2010); advise everyone to avoid them.
Irritation, trauma or inflammation (folliculitis within a mole).
Rarely melanoma arising in a naevus.
Halo phenomenon (depigmented ring).
Benign and stable; most change slowly with age. Removal is only for diagnosis or symptoms; cosmetic removal is not NHS-funded.

pearls: Teach monthly self-examination using a partner or mirror, and photographs on the phone.
Immunosuppressed patients (transplant, biologics, methotrexate) and those on **BRAF inhibitors** can develop new or eruptive naevi. Refer lesions that look new or atypical.

Patients ask "can't you just shave it off?" Explain that removing a whole mole is necessary for an accurate diagnosis, and that cosmetic shaves may leave pigment that regrows (recurrent naevus, which then mimics melanoma.
"A tan is your skin's damage response." People with many moles, red hair or freckles, a family history, or a history of sunburn should never use sunbeds.
Check that sunscreen is applied in an adequate amount (about 2 mg/cm²: roughly 6–8 teaspoons for the whole adult body) and reapplied. Most people apply a quarter to a half of this.
